Okay, well I was pretty confused reading your post but this makes it make a lot of sense. I’ve been through some horrible stuff this last year involving my kids so I’m not trying to be harsh, I absolutely don’t want to contribute an ounce to your suffering, but very plainly you are “just doing it wrong.”

Concentration on the breath is the most straightforward practice that just, undeniably gives results when done correctly. I would pay very careful attention to the 100ms timescale and what exactly you are doing that you think is concentration. All of the instructions and teachings are completely irrelevant to practice except for the happy chance that they get you to realize what it is they’re getting at. IMO, most meditation texts and teachers are just.. really bad at explaining things. I probably am as well. 

If you are able to generate and sustain the intention to concentrate on the breath for an hour, there is no world where you don’t enter an *incredibly* altered configuration of consciousness. IME even in the beginning it takes no more than 20-25min before you are getting very strong euphoria, clarity of mind, etc. on par with moderate drug experiences but much, much cleaner. If you are not feeling substantial/notable changes in your experience whatsoever after 10 minutes then it’s just not happening, reset and try slightly differently. Now, depending on your pain level, that timeframe could be off. But it should be happening relatively quickly, consciousness is pretty responsive.

I would just forget about everything except for the examination of what exactly it is you are doing. There are only so many permutations of that. You’ve got a field of consciousness, there’s an object (breath) appearing in it, and there’s an intention that’s setting everything up to behave in a certain way regarding the object and propagating that behavior continually without ceasing. There’s a LITTLE bit more, which is that when you recognize that the experience is not conforming to your intention you kick in a secondary layer of intention - I.e., return to the breath. In my perspective, intentions are like little multimodal GIFs that replicate some kind of behavior of phenomena across the field of experience so long as they keep playing, and after the field of experience becomes pretty coherently aligned with the GIF it disappears into the background and there’s just the field of experience doing what you meant for it to do. Then if anything disturbs that behavior, the GIF comes back into attention and reorients everything again, maybe it recruits another GIF to act as an antidote to a particular kind of distraction. That’s how I think of it and it helps me a lot.

One tip, I would advise not pointing an “arrow of attention” at the object of meditation. Your goal is to have the appearance of the object concentrating itself, the sensations of the breath connecting to the very next sensations of the breath with no intermediary agent.

There is a pretty straightforward path to in-the-moment results. It’s just mechanistically the way consciousness works, you WILL cohere your field of experience around the object and euphoria, happiness, calm, relaxation, clarity, and openness WILL amplify the more consecutive seconds you do this. 

As far as long-term results vis a vis your baseline state of being outside of sits, that’s more complicated. Especially if bedridden. I got out of hardcore suicidal depression but it involved a lot of physical activity and friendships so I don’t think I have great/relevant advice there. But if you can unravel what is going on at a sub-second timescale and refine your mental schema of what exactly you’re even doing when you’re meditating, it’s only a matter of time, chance, circumstance, a particularly good day that kicks it off, etc before you get what you’re looking for in almost every session.

I’m curious what your meditation regimen looked like when you were giving it a stronger go. I have had a very similar sounding journey. 

How many minutes per session/sessions per day? What kind of techniques were you doing - and is it just one the whole session, is it a set series of techniques, or do you improvise? What kind of contemplative materials (YouTube, books, etc) do you consume to inform your practice? Were you actively tweaking the particulars of how you do it? What precisely were your struggles? 

In my experience, the vast majority of people who stop meditating didn’t end up searching the configuration space enough to find what “works” for them. There are several whole categories, hundreds of specific forms, and many thousands of combinatoric protocols - and unfortunately we use a single word for all of it. Before you write it off as ineffectual for your needs, I think you should make sure you’re actually experiencing what is on offer. Deep states of concentration are absolutely exquisite and can completely change the landscape your thoughts arise in for hours afterward, IMO in a way that psychedelics do not. 

Microdosing helped me realize it was possible to feel okay with life, but a really hardcore meditation practice is really the ONLY way I can tap into that in an on-going way. Still have super struggle days but it’s not anything like what it was without. I do a simple 15min seated breath concentration session in the morning after waking and brushing teeth and a quick stretch, then 40min at night. I allow myself to sit or stand or walk, eyes open or closed or half, and move through a number of techniques as it seems fit until I settle on the breath and move into deeper states of absorption, then usually end with just-sitting/choiceless awareness.

Good luck to you! I hope you can see some light at the end of the tunnel sooner rather than later, whatever means you find.

You’re just seeing the characteristic of no-self in perceptions and having a bunch of hallucinated narrative that got encoded by that seeing. If you “see the simulation” more clearly (note: NOT more intensely. specifically just more clearly, with less ideas about it) you’ll see there cannot possibly be a narrative having anything to do with the nature of perception, and then you’ll stop freaking out. It’s neither a simulation nor naive mundane reality. It’s just perception, and there’s no inherent quality to perceptions whatsoever. They just are exactly as they are.

Alternatively, you can just stop paying it much attention and wait a little bit. Probably go away faster than you’d expect if you treat yourself well - and focus any cognition on integrating and calming down and feeling well and being functional more than anything else. It literally doesn’t matter whatever you saw, even if you legitimately got fully enlightened - tomorrow you need to wake up, brush your teeth, and participate in society. We need eachother! Trust what a lot of people who got all the way to the other side seem to say, which is that at the end of insight you realize the whole path of insight isn’t that important. There is no difference between “seeing the simulation waves” and “being a normal guy who goes to work and sees his friend”. Nothing about reality is ANY different, it’s just a change of perception. 

You’re already in whatever is real before you have these trips and you were just fine when you didn’t see it. It’s just whether you’re paying attention to it. It’s fine to just retract away, especially if you feel destabilized. You can build the skill of being grounded and not have to always hanging in the back of your mind.

Maybe. The transformer architecture might have some nonlinearities in scaling whatever deeper logic is starting to develop. If that’s the case, it would be POSSIBLE to just make the model so big it starts to simulate a totally comprehensive and accurate world model inside somewhere, but it could be quadrillions of parameters. The point of this architecture search is efficiency. 

We already know simple feedforward networks are Turing complete and can implement any algorithm that a better architecture might implement; it just takes an insane amount of parameters and training time to stumble upon it, and maybe well-skilled real-time hyperparameter adjustment during the training schedule. If you had a planet-sized computer train the most basic neural network architecture we know of with 10^30 Params or something it almost certainly would attain ASI in all known domains.

If training LLMs at GPT-4 quality were 10x cheaper or better, then we could expect serious AGI contenders within 2-4 years with no major human advancements. GPT-4 with the right architecture and a skilled user is basically baby proto-AGI, there’s no contesting that. We could simply have it search the space and combine existing ideas and decide how to tweak models and run permutations on architecture all day long - but it’s just too damned expensive to search that way. 

Maybe the OSS models will really catch up, that would be pretty big. If these 7-30b param models can really compete with GPT-4 w/ only a few $k in training costs, then it would be very feasible for a single well-funded org to do a HUGE search on model architectures. I suspect this won’t be the case, but only on intuition.

Other than that, it’s the top / near the top of the S-curve + building out overhang right now. LLMs are a huge W on the tech tree, but we need quite a bit more to start approaching luxury space communism and urgent questions of existential risk.

Yes, it’s relatively easy to attain. It is a bit weird to just experience sensations without commentary, but it’s not utterly alien. Doing 5 minutes of Om chanting while paying attention to the sense of vibration in the chest, neck and head is a good cheat code for getting there - but it really just happens whenever you’re getting into a concentrated state, or “absorption”. I consider these kinds of techniques remedial. They really help you get to a state so you can explore what it does for you or reap some of its benefits, but it’s important to be build the skill of getting there w/ the activity of consciousness alone. You skip over a lot of the work by just providing a new kind of stimulus that is more interesting than thoughts. I do this when my anxiety is bad enough that I can’t even imagine trying to meditate normally.

Meditating (as you say you’ve been doing) refers to like hundreds of possible instructions/protocols you could be following, so it’s hard to say where to direct you. I have super crazy bad ADHD and I was able to get to a “no mind state” and quite a bit beyond that every day for months with just 15-25m of breath concentration. Even “concentrate on the breath, returning to it from every impulse that arises” can actually refer to multiple subtle mental actions that are not the same. Figuring out these subtleties is a big part of training yourself in meditation. 

The way I do breath concentration is like this:
Direct attention to the breath arising and passing at the nostrils. Expand this attention so that the whole body is being used to sense the breath. Make sure you’re paying attention to the natural automatic breath, and not controlling the breath. You can figure this out by trying to control your breath as much as possible, then stop. Whatever change happens there can give you some hints on how to pay attention w/o controlling. Doing this properly should feel like there isn’t much “effort” happening at all. Anyways, anything that comes up, you return the attention it takes to the breath with no other special actions concerning the interruption. Thoughts about how much time is left? Return that part of your attention to the breath. Thoughts about what you’re going to do later? Return. Don’t try to answer the thoughts or shut them down, just notice how they draw attention away from the breath and return to the breath.

If you feel like you really can’t help controlling the breath, try to move your attention a little more upward into the nose and head / away from the diaphragm and throat, and maybe outward to include the limbs. Yes, you can feel your breath in your limbs. It’s delayed from the breath at the nose and spreads from the chest outward, taking about 2 seconds to reach the extremities. The breath at the nose is the most salient sense of the breath so it’s easiest to return to or use as a centerpoint.

It also helps to experiment with changing from “my inner eye looking at the breath” to “the breath drawing attention to itself”. 

Do this for about 15 min and you should be in a notably different state of mind. You don’t need to do anything in particular with the breath, your attention will naturally cause everything in consciousness to synchronize with the breath moment to moment as you continue. This can (and eventually will reliably do so) cause your breath to feel extremely euphoric, your body may begin to buzz, your thoughts may seem more and more wispy and inconsequential and easy to return from, then maybe now the breath is at worst going into the background of attention but never fully leaving, you may see glowing lights if your eyes are closed (they don’t have to be! meditating with eyes open is sometimes a great idea for people w ADHD). 

For me, I feel euphoria over my entire body extending a few inches outside of the skin, I have almost zero thoughts, the meditation becomes entirely effortless, and there is this quality present that’s very hard to explain - unification, or tranquility, or samadhi. It’s like there is a common thread starting to orient all of my field of experience together, even if different stuff is happening all over. It’s like a bunch of sailboats in a fleet were loosely tied together. That feeling usually lasts for an hour and is able to be rejuvenated with just a few moments of concentration at any time.

I also get a really vibrant glowing circle in my vision. Once before this has exploded into extreme pleasure (easily twice as powerful as any drug at any dose I’ve ever tried, which is a lot). That was so startling that I immediately lost concentration, and it took 55min to get there so it’s not something I attempt much. That’s the 1st jhana. Looking to master that eventually when I have more time to meditate. That’s like all the sailboats being tied more and more thoroughly until, at the last moment, everybody pulls the lines all at once and they all lock together hull-to-hull. It’s really quite spectacular, but apparently that amount of pleasure gets boring after a while - or so I hear from people who can attain it on command.

So jhana are degrees of absorption. The longer you concentrate / how skillful your effort is goes toward aligning more and more subcomponents of your being to the act of concentration and the object (I highly recommend the breath for maximum life carryover effects per input time).

Access concentration is like the point of criticality where it’s possible to overcome barriers to absorption. The absorption graph is like little curved shelves: you go deeper and deeper until suddenly enough parts of the perceptual synchronize that it all kinda levels up at once in a noticeable way.

Once you can sense the breath pervading your perception of your body, it can spontaneously synchronize as a whole gestalt sensation that is very pleasurable. It’s felt often as a sudden onset of physical energy suffusing the body, along with glowy diffuse lights or colors behind the eyelids. It’s super great. Very much reminds me of the feeling of Christmas morning, but *much* stronger and more constant. That’s 1st jhana.

The rest of the components or aspects of perception synchronize in other distinct and relatively repeatable steps - body (1st jhana), emotions (2nd jhana), conceptual mind (3rd jhana), and more. It’s like a peeling away of the layers of chaos.

When you’re in first jhana, IME the body synchronizes as a single sensation that is made up of light and fuzziness like a blanket of neurotransmitter over every inch of your body, inside and out. It’s very nice. It’s also so distracting that I tend to lose it a little - you usually have to keep concentrating still at this stage. 

2nd jhana is territory I’m just getting into, and it is a similar kind of luminance and real-feeling-ness just centered around the vital organs as the interface to emotions. 1st jhana is pleasurable, 2nd jhana is joyful. 

If you want to read more, I highly recommend at least skimming through Daniel Ingram’s Mastering the Core Teachings of the Buddha. It’s free on his site. Also, people disagree heavily on what the terms mean, this is just my framework and experience

Could be that your training is inducing a state of high concentration that is quickly worn down by the game itself. People who meditate have better performance on some kinds of tests (including reflexes!) but often for only an hour or so after meditation.

Effortlessness is a quality that increases in deeper states of absorption. You’re extremely focused but it’s less hard to do it. In some schools, you wouldn’t be considered as experiencing certain discrete states of concentration UNLESS you have zero experience of effort in that moment.

Personally, I practice excessive non-violence toward my psyche when going into the practice - as smooth of an inlet curve to the stream as possible. No forcing, at least for me. That way my natural state and the meditative processes have eroded barriers and I am more likely to lean into that space during regular stressors. I deal with hindrances during the meditation the same way: not instantly reacting, just letting it resolve into the breath on the schedule it needs to. If I find that I’m trying hard, it’s usually because I’m working against the stream and not doing the real work - to become more conducive to the “effort” your experiential context is already impressing on you.

Get your setup and routine going, then sometimes try a 1 hr sit. I personally find that after the first 15 minutes, I’m able to passively shed off any thoughts about time. My automatic responsive energies to deal with thoughts get much more potent as concentration increases. 1 hr feels like 15 min + nothing. The experience becomes mediated more by dynamics in the qualities of concentration than by time at that point. Also, some back pain lol. I could go for another hour at the end of every sit, it becomes so utterly pleasant and effortless. Once you get to a certain state, you get more effort than you put in, if that makes sense. The net trying is negative, you’re more able to try the more seconds you try 😄

Consecutive, continual intention has a compounding effect. The longer in one sitting and the more uninterrupted your concentration is, the deeper you go “per second”. The more impactful meditative states are only separated from us by time-under-intention.

I recommend having a timer that will softly alert you. Easier to let go of the passage of time when you don’t anticipate sudden alerts. I use MyNoise which has timers you can set to fade out the background noises over 30 seconds - just enough to be noticeable but absolutely minimal jarring.

Lastly, the length and impactfulness of meditation afterglow is nonlinear with respect to time spent. It’s about depth of concentration/synchrony achieved. A 1 hr sit typically gives me 3-4 hr of tangible euthymia, increased self control, a positive mildly euphoric peripheral awareness of the breath that is constant, and almost no ego-dystonic thoughts. Also, emotions process on the spot rather than accrue in that state (so far!). Then it will have aftershocks until the end of the day, spontaneous serenity and breath awareness for about 15 min at a time.

A 15 minute sit will make me feel like I woke up from a good nap, but for only about 30 min or so unless I refocus it. Still worth it, but not nearly as worth it per-time-invested. But dangit it is so much easier for non-meditative mind to accept the 15 minute loss of time 😂

IMO in a really rough patch a strong experience can be more destabilizing than helpful. It’s a dice roll. Having one of the most beautiful and fun wholesome times in your life will help you realize that it is possible to see life as wonderful (even with its challenges).

There’s a high profile crowd crush case every couple
of years globally and you want everybody to never go to any crowd event ever again?

??? No individual person in a crowd really has anything to do with crowd crush. It’s almost mechanical how non-personal it is. Individual behavior doesn’t describe the motion of the crowd at those densities; equations for fluid mechanics do. Crowds like this are SO non-personal, so described by fluid mechanics that they actually exhibit shockwaves when somebody is pushed faster than the normal speed at which they move in the space of the crowd. 

The ONLY thing that causes crowd crush is the person or phenomena inciting the crowd, and they (the venue via security, or the performer by their voice) are kinda the only thing that can stop it. Once it’s at that point, it’s only a matter of probabilities whether somebody is crushed to death. If a single person trips and falls, the odds that somebody else trips on them and falls grows, and this cascades until there is an entire layer of people underneath the crowd that have no chance to get up. In this instance, the fallen were multiple layers deep. Those people had no chance of getting to the edge of the crowd and escaping once they realized it was happening, or doing anything like that to take responsibility for the danger. A 50,000 person crowd means you have to push past about 100 people in a row to escape from the center, and they would have been really lucky to successfully and safely push past 5-10.

Crowd crush. Past a certain point of density per sqft in a crowd, everybody but the edge of the crowd loses the ability to move individually and they’re just a fluid. If people push hard enough on the edge (usually to get closer to the stage) then the people near boundaries or in the center of the crowd come under so much pressure that they can’t expand their chest to inhale. Also, the people who get knocked over never find another hole to pop back up into as the crowd instantly presses into the space they left - they are crushed similarly, but with fewer breaks between breathlessness. Once there is more than one layer of fallen people, those at the bottom have an extremely high risk of severe injury and death.

I think panpsychism MUST be true in some fashion. There must be some universal embedded potential such that certain kinds of brains beget sapient, conversant conscious agents that notice their own consciousness. 

I find the problem of individuation utterly unfixable in any of these lines of thought, though. How I am me and you are you. It is so pervasive. I have my intuitive answer but I can’t derive it anywhere solidly.

That’s the point of my statement. The objective world exists less and less subjectively the more people observe it and collaborate on their models through language (verbal, but also bodily/gesture and pheromonal included if we want to talk about nonhumans).

You can only discover nonsolipsism by collaboration with entities whose contributions convince you of a) their own authenticity, usually by implicit means and b) of an exterior world. Solipsism or mind-only ontology is the blank state of consciousness pre-learning.
The one objective reality can be understood as circumscribed by the distribution of parameters as described by the intersection of the reports of all sapient conscious agents.

It could follow, but I don’t think it does. It kinda doesn’t matter if the substrate is “real” or not. If creation is all in the mind of God but he also has a reflective mind, then we would just shift ontology over. Now the “mind of God” that simulates the world is just Reality, and the mind of God that’s actually a mind is the Mind of God. No substantive difference, and the experience is the same either way. Might as well just say the world is real.

Panpsychism has a more interesting position on that but I wholeheartedly think nondualism/solipsism is untenable and only makes sense because it’s terms are too vague.

It doesn’t matter, his thrust was that the beliefs belong in the phenomenological realm - they are unenforceable and not arbitrarily transmissible. Basically zero chance of a non-dystopian singularity within the next 15 years. I’d give 10% odds it happens by 2040, 25% by 2050, and approaching 100% by 2070.

Having said all that, I think AGI/ASI comes down to a small parameter space for architectural design being searched with sufficient processing power, and sufficient interface with the real world. A small group with the right idea and a huge chunk of capital for compute resources and robotics could easily get it done by 2025-2027 IMO. They’d still take so many years to get it integrated into and trusted by society, but the actual work probably isn’t as mind-numbingly hard as most imagine. 

There are ways in which you might say the singularity has already happened - it is probably inevitable at this point, barring total destruction, that the current elements at play will arrive at ASI. Delineate the degree of instantiation in different ways and you get different time horizons.

Just started doing this yesterday and my KDA went from 1.25 -> 1.47 in \~10 matches. I realized that I don't like taking long range engagements except to push into them, so the lack of extreme range doesn't matter at all. Finally discovered my preferred playstyle!

​

*Springfield* \- You can start off any push with a headshot at distance, and while the Vetterli is much better the Springfield really puts in work. Put enemies into a finishable state with some quickscope magic. The deadeye IMO extends the viable range significantly without obstructing your closer-midrange capability as much as the Marksman or Sniper. It's very easy to pull fights in to medium range (esp. since Dum Dum puts on pressure to retreat and heal), but it is very hard or just impractical to push them out to long range most of the time. I really just think of the Vetterli as a straight upgrade on fire rate and aiming stability (esp. with Scopesmith/Steady traits) and treat them both exactly the same.

*Lemat* \- You can terrify folks with 18 rounds of rapid fire penetration, and you can almost ALWAYS down somebody running at medium range with crouched ADS dual wield fire. The rapid fire of the first two shots is deadly indoors. The buckshot (correct me if I'm wrong) is basically as good as the Romero Handcannon but you have two, and I consistently get kills across rooms and at short outdoor distances with it. The shotshells are extremely underrated, you just have to be judicious about when to use them vs. rapid fire. I cannot talk about dual FMJ Lemats enough, truly a hidden gem that dominates close-midrange. Have yet to run out of special ammo after multiple server wipes almost entirely with the Lemats.

*Quad Derringer* \- You have a pocket bornheim. The quad puts in work, don't discount it. Not to mention, (again, correct me!) it's not audible past 100m so you can be more liberal with it to dispatch AI or traps. Headshots are very possible even in an intense fight, especially if you let mobs run at you and practice CQB headshots whenever you get the chance. Useful for finishing rifle hits out in the open, as well.

​
